title: Nehemiah 2:1–8
context: Nehemiah 2:1–8 describes how, in the month Nisan of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah’s sad face before the king leads to the king’s question, a silent prayer, and a request to be sent to rebuild the city of his fathers’ tombs. The king, with the queen sitting beside him, grants the request and a set time, and Nehemiah asks for letters to the governors beyond the River and to Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest for timber. The queen is not named, and attempts to identify her go beyond the text. The question of how Chislev (1:1) and Nisan (2:1) fit within the same twentieth year is noted at 1:1–3 and left open. The phrase “the good hand of my God on me” (2:8) echoes Ezra 7:6, 9, 28, where the king grants Ezra’s request according to the LORD his God’s hand on him. Both traditions read the scene as shared ground: Nehemiah acts with courage and careful planning, and he attributes the king’s favor to God.

verses.text: In the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, when wine was before him, I picked up the wine, and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad before in his presence.
verses.arminianNotes:
In Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah serves wine to the king; he had not been sad before in the king’s presence. The relation of Nisan here to Chislev in 1:1 is discussed and left open.

Arminian readers note the months that pass between the news and this moment, and they see Nehemiah continuing in faithful duty while he waits for an opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the opportunity comes in God’s timing rather than Nehemiah’s, and they see the waiting period as part of God’s ordering of events. The phrase about not being sad before suggests that a servant’s sorrow before the king was unusual and risky.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: The king said to me, “Why is your face sad, since you are not sick? This is nothing else but sorrow of heart.” Then I was very much afraid.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king asks why his face is sad when he is not sick, and says it must be sorrow of heart, and Nehemiah is very much afraid. His grief is now visible to a powerful ruler.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah’s fear is honest and natural, and they see courage not as the absence of fear but as faithful action in spite of it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God bringing the matter into the open through the king’s own question, so that Nehemiah does not need to force the conversation, and they note that fear and faith can be present together in God’s servants.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about honest fear and the opening God provides.

verses.text: I said to the king, “Let the king live forever! Why shouldn’t my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers’ tombs, lies waste, and its gates have been consumed with fire?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah answers, “Let the king live forever! Why shouldn’t my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers’ tombs, lies waste, and its gates have been consumed with fire?” He speaks respectfully and carefully.

Arminian readers note the wisdom of his words, which honor the king and describe the city in personal terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Nehemiah does not yet name Jerusalem, and they see a tactful choice of words, especially if the king’s earlier order to stop the building lies in the background (compare Ezra 4:21).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: wisdom and honesty can work together when speaking to those in authority.

verses.text: Then the king said to me, “What is your request?” So I prayed to the God of heaven.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king asks, “What is your request?” and Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven before answering. The prayer is brief and silent, set between question and answer.

Arminian readers see a man who has already prayed for months turning to God again in the moment of decision, an example of continual dependence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the brief prayer rests on the long prayer of chapter 1, and they see Nehemiah acknowledging that the king’s heart and the outcome belong to the God of heaven.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about prayer in the midst of action, and they do not use it to reopen the question at Joshua 10:14.

verses.text: I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, I ask that you would send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers’ tombs, that I may build it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks, if it pleases the king and if his servant has found favor, to be sent to Judah, to the city of his fathers’ tombs, to build it. The request is bold but respectful.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah offers himself for the task, a willing and costly choice to leave a secure position for the sake of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Nehemiah’s request takes the form of humble petition to an earthly king while resting on the prayer he has just offered to the heavenly King, and they see both as means God uses.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: faithful service combines courage, respect for authority, and a clear sense of calling.

verses.text: The king said to me (the queen was also sitting by him), “How long will your journey be? When will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king, with the queen sitting by him, asks how long the journey will be and when he will return, and it pleases him to send Nehemiah, who sets him a time. The queen is not named, and the text does not explain why her presence is noted.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah has prepared a plan in advance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king’s favor as the answer to Nehemiah’s prayer for mercy in the sight of this man (1:11), and they note that the length of the time set is not stated here (compare 5:14; 13:6).

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and avoid speculation about the queen or the exact time agreed.

verses.text: Moreover I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah;
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah asks for letters to the governors beyond the River, so that they will let him pass through until he comes to Judah. He thinks ahead about the journey.

Arminian readers note that trust in God does not exclude careful preparation, and they see Nehemiah taking responsible steps to secure safe passage for himself and those with him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the request a recognition that God works through ordinary means such as official documents and royal authority, and they note that Nehemiah uses the king’s favor for the good of God’s people.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about wise planning in the service of God’s purposes, held together with dependence on him.

verses.text: and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel by the temple, for the wall of the city, and for the house that I will occupy.” The king granted my requests, because of the good hand of my God on me.
verses.arminianNotes:
He also asks for a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest, for timber for the gates of the citadel by the temple, the city wall, and his own house; the king grants his requests “because of the good hand of my God on me.” Compare Ezra 7:6, 9, 28.

Arminian readers note the detailed planning and Nehemiah’s grateful acknowledgment of God’s help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Nehemiah credits the king’s favor to the good hand of God, and they see the phrase as a confession that God governs the decisions of rulers for the good of his people. The location of the king’s forest is not stated.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s favor and human planning together.
